entities.name: COPE
entities.notes: The body most publishers cite, unrevised since 13 February 2023. Its separate discussion document on AI in editorial decisions dates from September 2021, before ChatGPT was released. The position statement places a duty on authors and assigns them liability; it contains no instruction to editors on what to do with a disclosure once received. Live publicationethics.org returns 403 to automated clients, so this record is verified against a dated Internet Archive capture.

sources.note: Live publicationethics.org returns 403 to every automated client (Cloudflare). This is a dated Internet Archive capture of the same page. The corresponding live policy was re-read on 15 October 2026; fixed archive captures are retained as evidence and do not establish current live freshness.

policies.conditions: Methods placement, naming the tool — three years before ICMJE said the same. Note the scope: it already covers collection and analysis of data.

evidence.quote: Authors who use AI tools in the writing of a manuscript, production of images or graphical elements of the paper, or in the collection and analysis of data, must be transparent in disclosing in the Materials and Methods (or similar section) of the paper how the AI tool was used
Authors are fully responsible for the content of their manuscript, even those parts produced by an AI tool, and are thus liable for any breach of publication ethics.

policies.conditions: The statement explicitly extends to "the collection and analysis of data".

evidence.quote: Authors who use AI tools in the writing of a manuscript, production of images or graphical elements of the paper, or in the collection and analysis of data, must be transparent in disclosing in the Materials and Methods (or similar section) of the paper how the AI tool was used

policies.conditions: A load-bearing negative. The position statement says nothing whatsoever about what an editor should do with a disclosure once received.

metadata_inconsistency.summary: The page states 'Last reviewed 13 February 2023' and carries a 2024 copyright line, while its DOI was deposited with Crossref on 2024-08-20. Cite it as reviewed February 2023, DOI deposited 2024.

entities.name: eLife
entities.notes: The natural experiment. The only organisation recorded here that permits reviewers to use AI — because its reviewed-preprint model means the manuscript is already public, so the confidentiality reason other publishers give does not apply. Remove that reason and the ban has nothing to stand on: the rationale, not the technology, is doing the work. Disclosure is nonetheless required. eLife is also the only organisation here addressing editors using AI to find reviewers.

sources.note: Since at least 2026-09-11 the URL redirects to the eLife submission system (elife-rp.msubmit.net, reviewer instructions); text unchanged. The public reviewer-guide URL is kept as the citable address.

policies.conditions: Permitted because the confidentiality rationale does not apply to an already-public reviewed preprint — but disclosure is mandatory. An earlier version of this record quoted only the subordinate clause and wrongly recorded disclosure as not addressed.

evidence.quote: While we do not prevent the use of generative artificial intelligence tools within the review process, editors and reviewers remain accountable for their contributions and the contents of their reviews. If generative AI tools are used by editors or reviewers, this must be disclosed.

policies.conditions: The only entity found that addresses editors using AI to source reviewers.

evidence.quote: If generative AI is used by editors to source suggestions for potential reviewers, we expect the usual due diligence

policies.conditions: eLife's image expectations are not stated on the reviewer-guide page held here. Third-party accounts describing eLife as banning AI figures are unsupported by this source.

entities.name: Elsevier
entities.notes: Rewrote its journals policy in June 2026, permitting reviewers supportive use of private AI tools. Its BOOKS policy previously used a URL ending 'in-the-review-process' and forbids editors using AI to evaluate material — secondary sources routinely quote that page as if it were the journals policy. Cell Press, an Elsevier imprint, is reported to serve superseded 2023 wording; Cell Press is not yet a record here. Re-read on 2026-09-11 against the text signed off on 2026-08-21: the record had captured five axes of a policy that rules on ten. Added writing, research-process, explanatory-image, data-visualisation and passing-off axes with quotes, and the 18 August 2026 Elsevier Connect announcement as a source.

sources.note: The slug says 'review process' but the page is Elsevier's BOOKS policy (13 mentions of book/chapter, zero of 'journal' in lower case). Secondary sources routinely quote it as if it were the journals policy. It is not. Recorded until 2026-09-11 as https://www.elsevier.com/about/policies-and-standards/the-use-of-generative-ai-and-ai-assisted-technologies-in-the-review-process, which now redirects here.
Elsevier Connect post announcing the updated journals policy, dated 18 August 2026; the policy page itself states 'Policy updated June 2026'.

policies.conditions: Exemption is withdrawn where changes go beyond basic correction.

evidence.quote: Basic checks of grammar, spelling and punctuation do not need a declaration statement

policies.conditions: Output must be checked by a competent bilingual human.

evidence.quote: by a person who has a good understanding of both languages

policies.conditions: Reversed in June 2026. Permitted only with a "private" AI tool as Elsevier defines it; disclosure to authors is mandatory. Uploading the manuscript remains prohibited.

evidence.quote: Reviewers should not upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into an AI tool
AI tools may therefore only be used in a supportive capacity, for example to improve the language and structure of a review report, or to assist with a background literature search

policies.conditions: The two policies disagree. The journals policy states Elsevier's editors have AI tools for reviewer identification and duplicate detection; the books policy forbids editors using AI to evaluate material at all. Neither tells an author which tools ran on their manuscript.

evidence.quote: Our editors have access to AI tools that assist in identifying relevant reviewers, matching the scope of submissions, and detecting duplicate submissions.
Generative AI or AI-assisted technologies should not be used by editors to assist in the evaluation of authors' material/ manuscript

policies.conditions: No threshold for triggering review, no duty to notify the author, and no route of appeal is stated. The quote records what is granted instead: editorial discretion.

evidence.quote: Authors may be asked to provide documentation of their AI use and the original, unprocessed images for editorial assessment.

policies.conditions: Author-facing policy mentions image forensics only. Check Integrity was expanded to nearly 2,000 journals in March 2026 without appearing in the author policy.

Separate AI declaration statement at submission, published with the article; basic grammar and spelling checks exempt, substantive changes to structure or content must be declared. Output must not replace the authors' own judgement, analysis or interpretation.

evidence.quote: Authors should disclose the use of AI tools for manuscript preparation in a separate AI declaration statement included in their manuscript upon submission.
Although AI tools may support your writing process, they must not replace your own scientific judgement, analysis, interpretation or intellectual contribution.

policies.conditions: Described 'in a reproducible manner' in Methods with model or tool, version and developer. The policy names AI-assisted imaging and predictive modelling as examples; agentic or autonomous workflows are not named.

evidence.quote: Where the use of AI tools forms part of the research design or research methods, the use of the tools must be described in a reproducible manner in the Methods section.

policies.conditions: Explanatory images only (flow charts, decision trees, timelines, schematic illustrations, workflow diagrams); tool, version and use disclosed in each caption and in the AI declaration.

evidence.quote: Authors may use AI tools to support the creation of certain types of explanatory images for publication, such as flow charts, decision trees, timelines, schematic conceptual illustrations, or experimental workflow diagrams.
The use of AI tools should be disclosed in the caption of each image (including the specific tool, version, and how the tool was used) and in the general AI disclosure statement in the article.

policies.conditions: Only where the visual is directly derived from underlying data via reproducible methods reported in Methods; tool, version and developer disclosed there.

evidence.quote: AI tools may be used to support the creation of data visualizations only when the visual output is directly derived from underlying data.
Where AI tools are used in the generation of data visualizations, authors should disclose the name of the model or tool, the version used, and the developer or manufacturer, in the Methods section.

policies.conditions: Covers fabricated results, invented or altered data, figures not faithfully derived from data, and primary research images (microscopy, blots, scans, patient images).

evidence.quote: AI tools must not be used to fabricate results, invent or alter underlying data, or generate figures that are not faithfully derived from the underlying data and methods used in the research.
AI tools must not be used to create or alter images that represent primary observed or experimental data that were not directly obtained in the research.

coherence.summary: The books policy forbids editors using AI to evaluate material, while the journals policy states Elsevier's editors have access to AI tools that identify reviewers and match submissions. Both are live; the books policy sits behind a URL ending 'in-the-review-process'.

metadata_inconsistency.summary: The policy page's own footer states 'Policy updated June 2026', while Elsevier Connect announced 'Elsevier has updated its generative AI policies for journals' on 18 August 2026. Either the August post is a late announcement of the June revision or the page changed again without its date line. Cite the page as updated June 2026 per its own statement.

entities.name: ICMJE
entities.notes: Updated January 2026 with a whole new Section V. Files AI structurally INSIDE contributorship (II.A.4, directly after Non-Author Contributors) and NOT under conflicts of interest — which refutes the naive claim that guidance treats AI use as a competing interest. Section V.C is the first text anywhere obliging journals to disclose their own AI use.

policies.conditions: Disclosure duty at submission, in the cover letter AND in the work itself.

evidence.quote: Authors who use such technology should describe, in both the cover letter and the submitted work in the appropriate section if applicable, how they used it.

policies.conditions: The tool-and-version instruction already exists here. But the required fields are dimensioned for a citation, not a trace — adequate for a paragraph, meaningless for forty tool calls. The document contains zero occurrences of agent, agentic or autonomous, against four of "chatbot", under a Section V titled "Use of AI in Publishing".

evidence.quote: including the tool used, version, and prompts where applicable.

policies.conditions: Section V.C. The first obligation anywhere on journals to disclose their own AI use — which converts the author/publisher asymmetry from an ethical complaint into a measurable compliance gap.

evidence.quote: Journals should have a policy for the use of AI in the review process and should make all editors, reviewers, and authors aware of this journal policy.

policies.conditions: No threshold for triggering review, no duty to notify the author, and no route of appeal is stated. The quote records what is granted instead: editorial discretion.

evidence.quote: Editors should be vigilant that authors may not disclose AI use when queried.
Nondisclosure of AI use may require corrective action and may be construed as misconduct in some circumstances

metadata_inconsistency.summary: The HTML title tag reads 'January 2025' while the URL and page body both say January 2026. Harmless to a reader; it will mislead an automated scraper.

entities.name: ISTIC Guideline
entities.notes: Three editions: v1.0 September 2023, v2.0 September 2024, v3.0 December 2025, co-signed by Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, Taylor & Francis, Wolters Kluwer and Cambridge University Press. It requires disclosure detail that English-language policy does not, including archiving AI session records. NOT a standard: it explicitly disclaims precedence over publisher policy and carries no standard number. A separate Chinese national guidance project on the same subject is registered and still under approval. Several verdicts here rest on the English v3.0 text; the Chinese edition is quoted where the English does not cover the point.

policies.conditions: Six mandatory disclosure elements: the user; the AI system WITH VERSION NUMBER; the date and time of use; the prompts and questions used; the parts of the text written or co-written by AI; and the ideas arising from that use. Version 3.0 additionally requires naming the specific sections assisted, quoting the actual prompts, and ARCHIVING THE AI SESSION RECORDS AS AN ATTACHMENT.

evidence.quote: detailing disclosure and declaration requirements during the manuscript submission phase

policies.conditions: AI must not generate research hypotheses, write the whole paper, interpret data or draw scientific conclusions. Non-disclosure was made misconduct in v2.0 — over a year before ICMJE said the same.

evidence.quote: 研究人员使用AIGC直接生成的稿件文字等资料必须提供明确的披露和声明，否则将构成学术不端行为。

policies.conditions: NOTE: this sentence comes from the third edition's list of changes, not from its normative text. It establishes that the guideline addresses journal, publisher and reviewer responsibilities — not what those responsibilities are.

evidence.quote: emphasizing the responsibilities of relevant parties (including journals/publishers and reviewers) during the review process.

policies.conditions: Reported in research notes but not locatable in the English v3.0 text held here. Recorded as not addressed rather than asserted without a quote.
Reported in research notes but not locatable in the English v3.0 text held here. Recorded as not addressed rather than asserted without a quote.
Experimental images — Western blots, cytometry, histology — must not be AI-generated.

evidence.quote: For example, experimental images in the biomedical �ield—such as Western blot analysis diagrams, cell technology analy- ses, and tissue cell staining diagrams—must be obtained from genuinely conducted experimental research.

entities.name: JAMA Network
entities.notes: Publisher of JAMA and the JAMA Network specialty journals (American Medical Association). One instructions-for-authors page serves every title, so the AI rules are network-wide. Revised guidance was published as an editorial on 2026-08-10 (Flanagin, Perlis, Bibbins-Domingo; doi:10.1001/jama.2026.16613, Crossref-verified 2026-09-11) with a table grading fourteen use types; the instructions page was updated 2026-07-29 to add the prohibition on drafting Opinion pieces, Letters and Comments. Alongside Science / AAAS it is one of two publishers here ruling on AI-drafted responses to reviewers (not permitted). Live jamanetwork.com returns 403 to automated clients; both sources are dated Internet Archive captures.

sources.note: Live jamanetwork.com returns 403 to automated clients. Dated Internet Archive capture; the page states 'Last Updated: July 29, 2026'. The previous capture (2026-07-01) lacks the Opinion/Letters/Comments prohibition, so that rule dates from July 2026. The corresponding live policy was re-read on 15 October 2026; fixed archive captures are retained as evidence and do not establish current live freshness. The live instructions show Last Updated: September 8, 2026; the July date above describes the retained capture. The recorded AI provisions remain present.

Flanagin A, Perlis RH, Bibbins-Domingo K. Updated Guidance for Author Use of AI in Medical Publication. JAMA, published online 2026-08-10, doi:10.1001/jama.2026.16613. Carries the acceptable-use table and the Box reproduced in the instructions. Dated Internet Archive capture. The corresponding live policy was re-read on 15 October 2026; fixed archive captures are retained as evidence and do not establish current live freshness.

policies.conditions: Not permitted at all for Opinion manuscripts, Letters to the Editor and online Comments ('human insights are prioritized'). Acknowledgment must name tool, version, manufacturer, dates of use, what it was used on, and confirm author responsibility.

evidence.quote: Use of AI, LLMs, chatbots, or similar technologies to assist with content creation, revision, and formatting must be reported in the Acknowledgment section.
Use of AI, LLM, and chatbots to draft Opinion manuscripts, Letters to the Editor, and Online Comments is not permitted.

policies.conditions: Only after the initial text is written by humans.

evidence.quote: Note this guidance does not apply to basic tools for checking grammar or spelling.
Use of AI tools and software to check grammar and spelling or for translation is permitted, but only after the initial text is written by humans.

policies.conditions: Table row; warns against entering content into public translation tools.

evidence.quote: Translation Yes, provided the use is fully described in the Acknowledgment section and authors check for accuracy and take full responsibility for all content

policies.conditions: The editorial's table grades this 'Discouraged'; the instructions say 'should not'.

evidence.quote: AI, LLM, and chatbots should not be used to generate or format references as these tools may cause problems with the accuracy and integrity of cited references; standard reference managers may be used instead.

policies.conditions: Scope is clinical images and clinical illustrations (and clinical video/audio); the sole exception is use as part of formal research design or methods, which must be fully disclosed. Non-clinical explanatory figures are not addressed.

evidence.quote: Submission of clinical images and clinical illustrations created or manipulated by AI, LLM, and chatbots is not permitted, unless part of formal research design or methods, which must be fully disclosed.

policies.conditions: Name and version number of the AI or software in the figure legend.

evidence.quote: Use of AI to generate graphic visualization of research data or results is permitted, provided that the AI or software (name and version number) used is included in the figure legend.

policies.conditions: Table row in the editorial.

evidence.quote: Presenting AI-generated data as if it were original research from non-AI sources No

policies.conditions: Follow the relevant reporting guideline; describe each use in Methods; for LLM studies give platform, version, manufacturer, dates and prompts; for ML give training/validation data, metrics, bias and subgroup analyses; data-sharing statement including code.

evidence.quote: Research Yes, provided the use is fully described in the Methods section and reporting guidance is followed and authors take full responsibility for all content

Describe how AI was used for specific aspects of the study (eg, to generate or refine study hypotheses, assist in the generation of a list of adjustment variables, create graphs to show visual relationships).

policies.conditions: For research use: prompts, their sequence and revisions, dates, platform and version in Methods. For manuscript preparation: tool, version, manufacturer and dates in the Acknowledgment. No requirement to archive session records.

evidence.quote: For studies using LLMs, provide the name of the platform or program, tool, version, and manufacturer; specify dates and prompt(s) used and their sequence and any revisions to prompts in response to initial outputs.

policies.conditions: Stated in the author-facing table; JAMA Network's separate reviewer instructions are not held here. The same table also bars AI-drafted author responses to reviewer and editor comments.

evidence.quote: Entering an author’s manuscript or the reviewer’s summary of the manuscript into an external AI tool or LLM is a violation of confidentiality

policies.conditions: A sanction is stated (rejection or post-publication correction) but no threshold for suspicion, no duty to notify the author and no route of appeal.

evidence.quote: If incomplete disclosure or failure to disclose use of AI is detected during the editorial process or after publication, content may be rejected or subject to postpublication corrective action.

policies.conditions: Both sources speak of non-disclosure being 'detected' but neither says whether AI-text screening is run or whether authors are told.

entities.name: PLOS
entities.notes: The AI section changed between the successful fetches of 11 September and 1 October 2026; the 15 October fetch matches the 1 October wording. It now expressly exempts language improvements from disclosure, recommends disclosure for translation, and addresses analysis code, figures and AI detection. Reviewer and editor disclosures must be available to authors. The policy distinguishes disclosure from undisclosed or unacceptable use; disclosure itself is not grounds for an adverse decision.

sources.note: No revision date is stated. A text change is bounded by the 11 September and 1 October 2026 fetches; it is not dated precisely. Re-read on 15 October.

policies.conditions: Exemption covers spelling, grammar and rephrasing for clarity or conciseness; it does not cover generating new intellectual content.

evidence.quote: We do not require disclosure of AI use for language improvements, such as to correct spelling or grammar, or to rephrase content for clarity or conciseness.

policies.conditions: Authors retain responsibility for accuracy and their own ideas. Name the tool, explain its use and affected content, and describe how outputs were checked. Methods and Acknowledgements are alternative locations; figure-specific use belongs in the legend.

evidence.quote: AI tools may be used to support development or revision of a PLOS submission.

Any AI use to generate or revise content for a PLOS submission, or to support research reported in a PLOS article, must be clearly disclosed as outlined in the AI use disclosures section of this policy.
For AI use by authors, disclosures should be in the body of the article, either in a dedicated section of the Methods, in the Acknowledgement section, or in the relevant figure legend(s).

policies.conditions: Disclosure is recommended to preempt concerns but is expressly not compulsory.

evidence.quote: If an AI tool has been used for language translation, we recommend this be disclosed in order to preempt concerns, but this is not strictly required.

policies.conditions: Illustrative figures must not misrepresent primary research, introduce invalid content or put sensitive data at risk. Check accuracy, copyright and licensing; disclose use in the legend.

evidence.quote: For example, authors can use AI-generated figures for illustrative purposes or to summarize results, but should be aware that depending on the AI tool’s terms and conditions any data uploaded to the tool may be ingested into the AI tool’s training dataset and exposed to future users.
Any AI use for figure preparation should be clearly disclosed in the figure legend.

policies.conditions: Figures summarizing results are allowed only when valid and faithful to the research outputs; disclosure belongs in the legend. This does not permit fabricating or misrepresenting primary data.

evidence.quote: For example, authors can use AI-generated figures for illustrative purposes or to summarize results, but should be aware that depending on the AI tool’s terms and conditions any data uploaded to the tool may be ingested into the AI tool’s training dataset and exposed to future users.
Any AI use for figure preparation should be clearly disclosed in the figure legend.

policies.conditions: Fabrication or misrepresentation of primary research data is a breach of publication ethics.

evidence.quote: The use of AI tools and technologies to fabricate or otherwise misrepresent primary research data is unacceptable and will be considered by PLOS to be a breach of publication ethics.

policies.conditions: Includes development of analysis scripts or software code. Name the tools, identify affected study components and explain output validation. Code generation belongs to this research-process axis, which STM excludes from code formatting.

evidence.quote: Any AI use to generate or revise content for a PLOS submission, or to support research reported in a PLOS article, must be clearly disclosed as outlined in the AI use disclosures section of this policy.
Do I need to disclose AI use for generation or development of analysis scripts or software code? Yes.

policies.conditions: Only support that preserves confidentiality and the reviewer’s own intellectual contribution is allowed. AI may not summarize or evaluate submissions. Reviewers disclose in the review form; editors in the decision letter, available to authors.

evidence.quote: AI tools can only be used in peer review for purposes that (i) do not place the confidentiality of manuscript content or data at risk, AND (ii) would not misrepresent the reviewer’s or editor’s own intellectual contributions.

For AI use by editors or reviewers, the disclosure should be in the review form or decision letter so that the information about AI use is available to authors when they receive their decision letter.

policies.conditions: PLOS describes vetted AI tools for submission checks, screening and integrity investigations. It does not promise an article-specific account of which internal tools ran. Editor decision-letter disclosure is recorded separately under reviewer use.

evidence.quote: PLOS uses AI tools to support submission checks, screening, and integrity investigations, and we may also integrate AI tools to further support our publishing processes, communications, and author services.

policies.conditions: The policy expressly allows AI detection at article level; it does not say every submission is screened or promise individual notification.

evidence.quote: We may use available AI detection tools in article-level checks or assessments, and we follow up if editors, reviewers, staff, or readers report concerns about undisclosed AI use.

policies.conditions: The AI section offers a journal-office contact for decision or review concerns, and says disclosure itself will not adversely affect the decision. It does not specify an investigation threshold, a notification duty or a formal appeal procedure. These quotations document the limited guidance that is provided.

evidence.quote: Will AI use disclosures negatively affect my article’s review or editorial decision? No.
If you have concerns about your submission’s decision or review comments, please contact the journal office.

entities.name: Science / AAAS
entities.notes: Publishes an AI-use matrix grading roughly seventeen use-cases, and, with JAMA Network, one of two publishers here ruling on using AI to respond to reviewers. Research notes record that a November 2023 blog post required full prompt disclosure and barred reviewer AI, and that neither requirement appears on the live page — but that blog post is not among the sources held here, so the comparison is reported as an observation, not evidenced on this site. The live page carries no revision date. Live science.org returns 403 to automated clients; this record is verified against a dated Internet Archive capture.

sources.note: Live science.org returns 403 to every automated client. This is a dated Internet Archive capture. The corresponding live policy was re-read on 15 October 2026; fixed archive captures are retained as evidence and do not establish current live freshness.

evidence.quote: Reviewers may not enter any part of the manuscript into an LLM or other AI tool because this could breach the confidentiality of the manuscript.
However, reviewers may use AI tools to revise their own writing, provided that the system does not save or use inputs to train the model and that such use is transparently declared in the review.

policies.conditions: Reviewers may revise their own writing if the tool neither saves inputs nor uses them for training, and they disclose this in the review. Entering any manuscript content remains prohibited. This corrects the former blanket prohibition in this record; the exception was already present in the stored source.
Prior editor permission required; exceptions case-by-case and disclosed at submission.

evidence.quote: AI-generated images and other multimedia are not permitted in the Science journals without explicit permission from the editors.

policies.conditions: No threshold for triggering review, no duty to notify the author, and no route of appeal is stated. The quote records what is granted instead: editorial discretion.

evidence.quote: Editors may decline to move forward with manuscripts if AI is used inappropriately.

policies.conditions: The AI-use matrix asks the editorial office to post its own AI tools on the journal website.
